options: SQL Server automatically converting many fine-grained row or page locks into a single table-level lock
SQL Server automatically splitting a table lock into many row locks
A DBA manually upgrading a shared lock to an exclusive lock
A setting that must be explicitly enabled before any locking occurs
questions.explain: Escalation is an automatic, built-in safety valve that trades granularity for lower overhead once a threshold is crossed.

questions.q: Roughly what threshold triggers lock escalation for a single statement on one table/index?
options: Around 5,000 locks
There is no threshold — it happens on every statement
Exactly 1,000,000 locks
Exactly 10 locks
questions.explain: SQL Server escalates to a table lock once a single statement's row/page locks on one table or index cross roughly the 5,000-lock mark.

questions.q: Why can a large batch UPDATE suddenly start blocking sessions it wasn't blocking a moment earlier?
options: It started with row-level locks that didn't bother anyone, then crossed the escalation threshold partway through and switched to a table lock covering every row
The batch UPDATE was rewritten mid-execution by the optimizer
Other sessions' queries became syntactically invalid
SQL Server randomly blocks sessions every 30 seconds regardless of locking
questions.explain: Escalation can happen mid-statement, turning a previously unobtrusive row-locking operation into one that blocks everyone via a table lock.

questions.q: Why does escalation make sense from SQL Server's perspective?
options: Tracking one table lock is far cheaper in memory and management overhead than tracking thousands of individual row locks
It eliminates the need for intent locks entirely
It only ever happens during off-peak hours
It always improves concurrency compared to row-level locking
questions.explain: Past a certain point, the overhead of maintaining huge numbers of fine-grained locks outweighs the concurrency benefit, so escalating to one table lock is cheaper to manage.

questions.q: What is a practical way to avoid triggering unwanted lock escalation on a large operation?
options: Run the operation twice so the second run uses cached locks
Disable all locking for the duration of the statement
Break the large batch operation into smaller batches, each comfortably under the lock-count threshold
Always wrap the entire operation in SERIALIZABLE isolation
questions.explain: Since escalation isn't a setting you can simply turn off, keeping each statement's lock count well under the threshold is the practical mitigation.
